prompt: Show me how stochastic gradient descent works. Let me change the learning rate and batch size to see what happens.

plan.title: Stochastic gradient descent: a noisy ball on an error bowl
plan.description: A ball moves step by step across a wireframe bowl. The bowl is an error surface over two model settings, and its height is the error. On each step the ball moves downhill along a noisy estimate of the slope, like one taken from a small random batch of data, and leaves a trail of up to 40 points. A faint second trail shows plain gradient descent, which uses the exact slope, from the same start for comparison. Change the learning rate and batch size to see the path go from smooth to jittery, or from slow to overshooting and diverging.
plan.reason: SGD makes sense once you see how step size and batch noise shape the path. Here you change both and watch the trail, the arrows and the error readouts respond together.

parameters.label: Show full-data gradient descent path for comparison

interactions: Learning rate: small values take short, slow steps. Larger ones move faster. Near the top of the range, steps overshoot and zig-zag, growing until the run ends as 'diverged'.
Batch size: at 1 the bright arrow and the path jitter a lot. Larger batches make the path smoother. At 64 the noise is zero, so the path is the same as plain gradient descent.
Comparison path toggle: shows or hides the faint trail of plain gradient descent, which uses the same learning rate and the same start.
Run and pause the steps, or advance one step at a time to see each noisy step move the ball.
Start from a new point: moves the ball to the next of a few preset starting spots on the bowl and clears both trails and the step count. Your settings stay as they are.
Orbit the camera to view the bowl from above, where you see level lines, or from the side, where height is error.
Readouts show the step number (out of 40), the error at the ball, the noisy batch estimate of that error, and the number of passes through the data (epochs = steps × batch size ÷ 64).
assumptions: This is an illustration: the bowl is a made-up error surface and the batch noise is simulated, not drawn from real data.
The error surface is an exact bowl over two settings. It is steeper in one direction than the other, and it is drawn as a wireframe of level lines and cross-sections.

Each step uses the exact downhill slope plus random noise from a fixed seed, so the same settings give the same run after Reset. The noise spread shrinks as batch size grows and is exactly zero at 64, like sampling a batch without repeats from 64 imaginary points.

The bright arrow at the ball shows the next step: the negative of the noisy slope, times the learning rate. The faint arrow shows the same step using the exact slope. The gap between the two arrows is the batch noise.
A run lasts at most 40 steps. Each trail keeps at most 40 points, one per step. A run ends early as 'diverged' if the ball leaves the drawn bowl.
On average, the noisy step points the same way as the exact one. But any single step can go uphill, so the error readout usually falls, though not on every step.
Changes to the learning rate or batch size apply from the next step.
limitations: Real networks have millions of settings and bumpy error surfaces. A two-setting bowl shows the effects of step size and batch noise, but not local minima or saddle points.
No real data is shown or used. The batch noise only copies how its spread depends on batch size.
Momentum, learning-rate schedules and optimizers like Adam are not included.
Speed is counted in steps. Larger batches cost more work per step in real training, and the scene does not show that.
plan.learningGoal: See that SGD steps downhill along a noisy estimate of the slope. Smaller batches make the path noisier, while the learning rate trades speed against overshooting and divergence.

authorDraft.title: Stochastic gradient descent: a noisy ball on an error bowl
authorDraft.description: A wireframe bowl of level lines and cross-sections stands for an error surface over two model settings; height is error. An orange ball steps downhill along a noisy batch estimate of the slope, leaving orange dots. A faint blue ball and dots show plain gradient descent from the same start. A red arrow at the orange ball shows its next noisy step; a faint blue arrow shows the exact step. Readouts give the step number, error, batch error estimate and epochs.

parameters.label: Show full-data gradient descent path for comparison

assumptions: Illustration only: the bowl is a made-up error surface and the batch noise is simulated, not drawn from real data.

Error E = 0.5·(w1² + 4·w2²), drawn as a wireframe: level lines at E = 1, 3 and 6 (the rim) and two cross-sections; height = 0.3·E. Plain GD is stable only for learning rate below 0.5 (2 ÷ 4), so it zig-zags near 0.4–0.5 and diverges above 0.5.

Noisy slope = exact slope + 1.2·√((64−B)/(63·B)) × Gaussian noise per setting, from a fixed seed: the spread is largest at B=1 and exactly zero at B=64, like sampling without repeats from 64 imaginary points.
Red arrow: the next step, −learning rate × noisy slope; faint blue arrow: the same with the exact slope. Both drawn at true length in setting units (scale 1), horizontal in the plane of the settings.

One step every 0.2 s while running; at most 40 steps and 40 trail dots per path. A run ends as 'diverged' when the ball's error exceeds 6, i.e. it leaves the rim; the comparison path stops at its last point inside the rim.

The noisy step points the exact way only on average, so the error usually falls but can rise on a single step. The batch error estimate is the error plus simulated noise of the same spread factor, floored at 0.
Changes to learning rate or batch size apply from the next step; Start from a new point keeps your settings and clears both trails and the step count.
